descriptionChirho: Intransitive Qal sense of inherent strength or courage, typically in exhortations ('be strong!') and stative descriptions ('was strong'). Arabic consistently uses تَشَدَّدَ / تَقَوَّى (reflexive strengthening verbs from Form V), Korean uses 강하라 (kanghara, 'be strong' imperative) and 강해졌다 (kanghaejyeotda, 'became strong'), Swahili uses kuwa hodari ('be brave/strong') or kuwa imara ('be firm'). This covers all Qal imperative, imperfect, perfect, and cohortative forms expressing the intransitive state of being strong or becoming strong, including future promises of strength.

Qal sense of prevailing or overpowering an adversary, implying competitive superiority rather than mere inherent strength. Arabic uses غَلَبَ / تَغَلَّبَ (ghalaba, 'to overcome, defeat') — a completely different root from the 'be strong' sense, confirming genuine polysemy. Korean uses 이겼다 (igyeotda, 'won/defeated') and 정복했다 (jeongbokaetda, 'conquered'). Swahili uses -shinda ('defeat, overcome'). This sense appears in narrative contexts of battle, contest, or forceful dominance.

Qal sense describing the intensification or severity of a condition (famine, battle, disease) rather than personal strength. Arabic uses اشْتَدَّ (ishtadda, Form VIII of sh-d-d, 'to become intense/severe'), distinct from تَقَوَّى used for personal strength. Korean uses 강해졌다 but context shows 'intensified'. Swahili uses -kuwa kali ('become fierce/severe'). This includes the sense of conditions worsening or growing in intensity.

Rare Qal sense of being physically caught or entangled (e.g., Absalom's hair caught in the oak). Arabic uses عَلِقَ (ʿaliqa, 'to be snagged, stuck') — entirely different from all other Arabic equivalents. Korean uses 걸렸다 (geollyeotda, 'got caught/snagged'). Swahili uses -kamatika ('get caught'). This is a genuinely distinct physical sense of being seized by an inanimate object.

Qal sense of pressing or urging someone insistently. Arabic uses ضَغَطَتْ (daghatat, 'she pressed/pressured') from the root ḍ-gh-ṭ, completely unrelated to strength vocabulary. Korean uses 재촉했다 (jaechokaetda, 'urged, pressed'). Swahili uses -sisitiza ('insist, press'). This represents social/interpersonal pressure rather than physical strength.

Rare Qal transitive sense with pronominal suffix meaning 'to strengthen someone'. Arabic uses يُقَوِّيهِ (yuqawwīhi, Piel-like causative in meaning). Korean uses 강하게 함 (ganghage ham, 'making strong'). Swahili uses -imarisha (causative). This is the Qal used transitively with a direct object, a marked usage.

Qal sense of recovering or regaining strength after illness. Arabic uses تَقَوَّى (taqawwā, 'grew strong again'). Korean uses 강하여졌다 (ganghayeojyeotda, 'became strong'). Swahili uses -pona ('heal, recover'). The Swahili -pona distinctly marks this as a medical/recovery sense rather than general strength.

Piel factitive/causative sense of making someone strong, encouraging, or supporting. Arabic uses قَوَّى (qawwā, Form II causative, 'to strengthen'), شَدَّدَ (shaddada, 'to fortify'), and شَجَّعَ (shajjaʿa, 'to encourage'). Korean uses 강하게 하다 (ganghage hada, 'make strong') and 격려하다 (gyeongnyeohada, 'encourage'). Swahili uses -imarisha (causative of -imarika, 'strengthen') and -tia nguvu ('give power') and -tia moyo ('give heart/encourage'). This covers all Piel forms that mean to strengthen, encourage, or support a person.

Piel sense of hardening, specifically of the heart (Pharaoh's heart) or face (obstinacy). Arabic uses قَسَّى (qassā, 'to make hard/callous') from the root q-s-w, categorically different from قَوَّى (strengthen). Korean uses 완고하게 하다 (wangohage hada, 'make stubborn'). Swahili uses -fanya kuwa mgumu ('make hard/difficult'). The Arabic root distinction (q-s-w vs q-w-y) is decisive evidence this is a separate sense from general strengthening.

Piel sense of repairing or restoring physical structures (temple, walls, city). Arabic consistently uses رَمَّمَ (rammama, 'to repair, renovate') — a completely distinct root from both قَوَّى and قَسَّى, confirming this is a genuine separate sense. Korean uses 고치다 (gochida, 'to fix, repair') and 수리하다 (surihada, 'to repair'). Swahili uses -karabati ('renovate'), -tengeneza ('fix, build'), and -rekebisha ('repair'). This construction-domain sense appears predominantly in Chronicles, Kings, and Nehemiah.

Piel sense of fastening, securing, or making firm physical objects (nails, pegs, idols). Arabic uses ثَبَّتَ (thabbata, 'to fix in place, fasten') from the root th-b-t, distinct from both رَمَّمَ (repair) and قَوَّى (strengthen). Korean uses 고정하다 (gojeong-hada, 'to fix/fasten'). Swahili uses -imarisha in a concrete/mechanical rather than personal sense. This is a technical/artisanal meaning about physically securing objects.

Hitpael reflexive sense of strengthening oneself or mustering courage. Arabic uses تَشَدَّدَ (tashaddada, Form V reflexive, 'to steel oneself') and تَقَوَّى (taqawwā, Form V, 'to grow strong'). Korean uses 강해졌다 (kanghaejyeotda, 'became strong') and 힘을 냈다 (himeul naetda, 'mustered strength'). Swahili uses -jiimarisha (reflexive causative, 'strengthen oneself') and -jitianguvu ('give oneself strength'). The Hitpael reflexive is semantically close to the Qal stative but emphasizes deliberate self-strengthening, an act of will.

labelChirho: Hifil: seize, grasp, take hold of
descriptionChirho: Hifil sense of physically seizing, grasping, or taking hold of a person or object. Arabic consistently uses أَمْسَكَ (amsaka, Form IV, 'to seize, grasp, hold') — a completely different root (m-s-k) from any of the strength vocabulary (q-w-y, sh-d-d). Korean uses 붙잡다 (butjapda, 'to grab, seize') and 잡다 (japda, 'to catch'). Swahili uses -shika ('grab, seize') and -kamata ('catch, arrest'). This is arguably the most semantically distinct sense of חזק, involving physical prehension rather than strength.

Hifil sense of holding fast or clinging to something in a sustained, ongoing manner — often metaphorical (holding to God, holding to deceit, retaining). Arabic uses تَمَسَّكَ (tamassaka, Form V reflexive of m-s-k, 'to cling, adhere to') and مُمْسِكٌ (mumsikun, active participle, 'one holding'). Korean uses 붙잡고 있다 (butjapgo itda, 'holding on to' — progressive aspect) and 붙들고 있다 (butdeulgo itda, 'clinging to'). Swahili uses -shikilia ('hold onto firmly', applicative of -shika). The Arabic Form V (tamassaka = reflexive/intensive holding) vs Form IV (amsaka = simple seizing) mirrors the Hebrew semantic distinction between sustained holding and momentary grasping.

Hifil sense specifically used for repairing buildings and walls, appearing prominently in Nehemiah as participial agent nouns ('repairers of'). Arabic uses مُرَمِّمِي (murammimī, 'repairers', active participle of رَمَّمَ). Korean uses 수리하는 자들 (surihaneun jadeul, 'those who repair'). Swahili uses wakarabati wa ('repairers of'). Though categorized under Hifil morphology, the semantic overlap with the Piel repair sense is strong, but the Arabic active-participle form and Nehemiah-specific usage distinguishes this as the Hifil counterpart.

Hifil sense of prevailing or being victorious, where the Hifil carries a resultative force beyond the Qal 'prevail'. Arabic uses يَظْفَرُ (yaẓfaru, 'to triumph') and يَتَقَوَّى (yataqawwā, 'to grow powerful'). Korean uses 이기리라 (igirira, 'will prevail'). Swahili uses -shinda ('defeat, overcome'). This Hifil sense overlaps with Qal 'prevail' but appears in prophetic/future contexts with a stronger causative-resultative nuance.

Hifil sense of urging or pressing someone insistently (e.g., Delilah pressing Samson). Arabic uses أَلَحَّتْ (aḥaḥḥat, 'she insisted/urged') from the root l-ḥ-ḥ, totally distinct from أَمْسَكَ (seize). Korean uses 붙잡았다 (butjabatda) but context shows persistent pressing. Swahili uses -sisitiza ('insist'). The Arabic root difference confirms this is a genuine sense distinction from physical seizing.

Hifil sense of strengthening or supporting another person, used in contexts of divine or human assistance. Arabic uses يُعِينُ (yuʿīnu, 'to help, assist') and مُقَوِّيهَا (muqawwīhā, 'her strengthener'). Korean uses 강하게 하다 (ganghage hada, 'make strong'). Swahili uses -saidia ('help, assist') and -tia nguvu ('give power'). This is the Hifil causative counterpart to Piel 'strengthen' but often carries the nuance of sustaining or upholding rather than active building-up.
